e.t: This word means “to buy,” describing the act of obtaining something by paying for it. It can refer to ordinary purchasing, whether someone buys food, oil, land, or other goods. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 30 times, so its basic sense is used across many kinds of buying situations. The word may appear in forms rendered “buying,” “buys,” or “to buy,” but the central idea remains a purchase or transaction.

e.t: Aeneas is a personal name, referring to a man identified by that name in the Greek New Testament. It is not a common noun describing an object, action, or quality, but a proper name used to identify one individual. The name appears twice, both times in Acts 9, where the English rendering is “Aeneas.” Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself simply identifies Aeneas by name.

e.t: This word means “locust” or “locusts,” referring to the insect. It is a noun used for actual locusts in the New Testament, including references in Matthew and Mark and symbolic imagery in Revelation. The word occurs four times in four New Testament verses. Its basic meaning remains the same wherever it appears, while the surrounding passage determines whether locusts are being mentioned as part of ordinary description or in prophetic imagery.

e.t: This word means “indescribable”: something so great, profound, or wonderful that words cannot adequately express it. It describes the limits of human speech rather than merely something difficult to explain. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Corinthians 9:15. Its precise force there belongs to the surrounding verse and passage, but its central sense remains a reality that cannot be fully put into words.

e.t: This word means “be bold” or “to bring forth boldly.” It describes speaking or acting with courage and openness rather than holding back. As a verb, it expresses the act of showing boldness, especially in what a person says or presents. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Romans 10:20; the surrounding verse context is needed to explain its particular force there. Its central idea remains confident, fearless expression.

This word means “newborn,” describing someone who has only recently been born. It is a straightforward descriptive word for a newly born child or infant, emphasizing the beginning of life rather than maturity or development. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Peter 2:2. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains someone newly born. e.t: This word refers to an asp or viper, a venomous snake. It is a noun naming this kind of dangerous creature, and its only occurrence in the Greek New Testament is in Romans 3:13. The wording there identifies asps as the image associated with what proceeds from the wicked, but the precise force of the expression belongs to that verse’s surrounding passage. The word itself simply denotes a venomous snake, specifically an asp or viper.

e.t: Achaia is the name of a region mentioned in the Greek New Testament. It identifies a location rather than an action, quality, or person. The word appears ten times in ten New Testament verses, beginning in Acts and continuing through 1 Thessalonians. Its repeated use as “Achaia” shows that it functions as a geographical name, while the surrounding verse determines what is being said about that region in each occurrence.

e.t: This word refers to a helper—someone who gives aid or support when help is needed. It can also describe a person or thing as helpful. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Hebrews 13:6, so its meaning is presented briefly rather than across many passages. The central idea is dependable assistance: a helper is one who comes alongside another to provide needed strength, support, or practical aid.

e.t: This word means “arm,” referring to the limb extending from the shoulder to the hand. It is a noun used for the human arm and occurs three times in the Greek New Testament. Its uses appear in Luke, John, and Acts, where the word retains this straightforward physical meaning. Scripture also uses the arm as a recognizable picture of strength and action, but the specific force of that imagery depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word itself names the bodily limb rather than an abstract quality or action.

e.t: Galilee is the name of a region mentioned throughout the New Testament. It functions as a geographic name, identifying a place rather than an action, quality, or object. The word appears 61 times in the Greek New Testament, from Matthew through Acts, and is consistently rendered as “Galilee.” Its precise significance in any passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning remains the name of this region.

e.t: Demas is a personal name, referring to a man mentioned among Paul’s companions and fellow workers. The name itself identifies the person rather than describing a quality, action, or spiritual principle. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times: in Colossians, Philemon, and 2 Timothy. Its precise significance in each passage comes from the surrounding verse and context, but lexically it functions simply as the person’s name, “Demas.”

e.t: This word means “to strain out”—to separate something from a liquid or mixture by filtering it. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 23:24, so its normal meaning is established by this single recorded use and its explicit lexical sense. The word focuses on removing or filtering something through a strainer, while the precise force of the action in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to mix,” describing the act of combining one thing with another. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming an object or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, once in Matthew and once in Luke, showing the same basic action in both places. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and comparison being made.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means a plan or plot, especially a carefully formed scheme. It describes an intended course of action rather than a spontaneous thought, and its usual sense can be either neutral or harmful depending on the surrounding context. In the New Testament, it occurs four times, all in Acts, where it is rendered “plot” or “plots.” The word therefore points to deliberate planning, often emphasizing hidden or hostile intent when the passage makes that clear.

e.t: This Greek verb means “to pour on” or “to pour on/over”—to direct a liquid onto something or someone. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or abstract idea. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Luke 10:34. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of pouring liquid onto or over another surface or person.

e.t: This word means “devoted,” describing someone set apart with steady readiness and commitment. It presents a person who gives focused attention rather than being distracted or divided. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 7:35. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central idea is clear: willing, attentive dedication toward a person, purpose, or responsibility. It describes settled commitment, not merely a momentary feeling or passing interest.

This word means “our,” expressing that something belongs to or is shared by the speaker and others. It is a possessive word, so it identifies a person, thing, or association as connected with a group that includes the speaker. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times. Its references include Acts, Romans, 2 Timothy, Titus, and 1 John, showing that the word can describe shared identity or association in different sentences. The precise force of “our” depends on the noun and surrounding words with which it is used.

e.t: This Greek word means “as” or “just as,” connecting one statement with another by showing comparison or correspondence. It helps relate an action, condition, or description to something else, so the reader understands that the second thought matches or illustrates the first. The word appears six times in the Greek New Testament, in Luke and Acts. Its exact force—whether emphasizing similarity, agreement, or the way something happens—depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central function is to join related thoughts through comparison.

In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, including uses translated with prevail. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains successful dominance over what resists it.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word refers to a dog, including the sense of a little dog. It is used for an animal rather than an abstract idea. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, all in two Gospel passages: Matthew 15:26–27 and Mark 7:27–28. These references show where it occurs, while the word’s basic meaning remains “dog” or “little dog.”

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to fade” or “to fade away.” It describes something gradually losing its strength, freshness, or visible vitality until it diminishes. The word can therefore express something that does not remain lasting or enduring, but weakens and passes away. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in James 1:11. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on fading and passing away.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to flog” or “to whip”—to strike someone repeatedly with a whip as physical punishment. It describes an action inflicted on a person, rather than a general feeling of pain or hardship. The word occurs seven times in the Greek New Testament, including passages that speak of people being whipped before or alongside other forms of punishment. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central meaning remains the act of beating with a whip.

e.t: This word means “moderately” or “not greatly,” describing something as limited in degree rather than extreme. It functions as an adverb, showing how much or to what extent something occurs. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Acts 20:12, so its normal lexical sense is clear even though the surrounding verse determines precisely what it modifies. The word presents a measured degree, neither suggesting a very large amount nor emphasizing intensity.

e.h: To Give Off a Bad Odor
e.t: This word means “to give off a bad odor” or “to stink.” It describes an unpleasant smell coming from something, especially when the odor is strong or offensive. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in John 11:39. As a verb, it expresses the action or condition of producing such a smell rather than naming the odor itself. Its basic meaning is straightforward: something smells so bad that the unpleasant odor is noticeable. The surrounding verse supplies the particular situation in which the word is used.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to sit beside” or “to sit by” another person. It describes someone seated alongside another, expressing physical position and closeness. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Luke 10:39. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the simple act of sitting beside or near someone. It does not itself describe the person’s attitude, purpose, or response; those details must come from the verse’s context.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “change” or “variation,” expressing the idea of something not remaining the same. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at James 1:17. Its lexical sense is broad enough to describe alteration or variation, but the surrounding verse determines what is changing in that particular use. This is a word about change itself, not necessarily about whether the change is good or bad.

e.t: This word means “to worry beforehand”: it describes concern arising in advance, before a matter must be faced or addressed. It focuses on the timing of the worry—earlier than the immediate situation itself—rather than simply describing concern in general. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Mark 13:11. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is to feel anxious or concerned ahead of time.

e.t: This word means “be poor” or “to be poor.” It describes poverty—the condition of lacking material wealth or resources. As a verb, it expresses being in that condition rather than naming a poor person or an object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Corinthians 8:9. Its exact force in that verse is clarified by the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the condition of being poor.

e.t: This word means “fever,” referring to a condition of elevated bodily heat and illness. It is used for a physical sickness affecting people in the New Testament. The word appears six times in the Greek New Testament, in accounts involving people who were ill. Its normal function is to name the illness itself, rather than the person suffering from it or the healing that may follow. The surrounding passage is needed to explain what happens in each individual reference.

It names something thrown away rather than treasured, and so can express strong rejection when used figuratively. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Philippians 3:8. Its exact force in that verse belongs to the surrounding sentence, but the word itself carries the plain sense of refuse or unwanted waste, not something worth keeping.

In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 8:7. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself emphasizes things growing together or alongside one another.

e.t: This word means “thirty,” the number that comes after twenty-nine and before thirty-one. It is used in the Greek New Testament as a specific number, whether counting a harvest’s yield, identifying a payment, or stating an amount. The word occurs 11 times in 11 New Testament verses, so its meaning remains consistent wherever it appears. The surrounding passage determines what is being counted or valued, but the number itself is simply thirty.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “plainly”: in a way that is open, clear, and not hidden. It describes how something is said or done so that its evident character is apparent rather than concealed. The word occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, each in a different verse. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains openness and clarity.

It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 6:1. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its basic meaning remains the physical action of rubbing. No broader figurative sense is established here.
